Executive Answer

How AbarVa gets smarter without becoming a black box.

AbarVa does not rely on vague model memory. It improves through governed knowledge layers: researched corpus, industry pattern packs, tenant context, client-approved overrides, and audited data loads. Moves and Source use those layers at runtime through brokers, retrieval, validation rules, and citations.

What changes for a client? Sharper decisions, not looser AI.

Every new rate card, modernization pattern, or client file must be parsed, validated, approved, versioned, and cited before it can influence an answer or estimate.

The five knowledge layers

Each layer has a different owner, update path, and trust level. The agent does not treat all text equally. Client-approved context outranks generic research; tenant-specific rate cards outrank benchmark rate cards; unsupported model guesses do not outrank evidence.

Layer What it contains Who can update it How agents use it
Research Spine Official sources, citations, confidence, extraction notes, open gaps. AbarVa research and engineering. Provides benchmark fallback and explains assumptions.
Global Corpus Reusable playbooks, standards, rate-card methods, modernization archetypes. AbarVa release process. Gives Moves and Source a structured operating model.
Industry Pattern Packs Healthcare, retail, airline, banking, and other industry-specific patterns. AbarVa plus expert review. Shapes domain-specific recommendations and evaluation criteria.
Tenant Context Client apps, vendors, systems, contracts, org roles, KPIs, evidence files. Client admins through Data Loads. Grounds answers in the client reality, not generic market advice.
Client Overrides Approved client rate cards, policy choices, mappings, exceptions, preferences. Client stewards and approvers. Overrides generic benchmarks and changes estimates for that tenant only.

How an update becomes available

Whether the update is a rate card, modernization research, a pattern pack, or a client data file, the path is deliberately controlled. The goal is speed with evidence, not uncontrolled training.

1

Register

A template or corpus object defines required fields, formats, owner, cadence, and what it unlocks.

2

Load

Admin uploads through Data Loads with tenant identity and operator attestation.

3

Protect

Files pass sensitive-data, malware, format, tenant, and size controls before parsing.

4

Parse

Deterministic parsers extract rows, facts, evidence, rates, or workload inventory. Formula cells are not trusted.

5

Validate

Required fields, ranges, enums, provenance, confidence, source dates, and tenant boundaries are checked.

6

Commit

Approved data is versioned into the data plane, indexed, and made available through brokered agent tools.

How it integrates into the data plane

Current Pattern

Parse first, commit only after gates pass

Data Loads first creates a validation preview. For context files, approved rows become tenant-scoped chunks/facts and are queued for embedding. For rate cards, the new path validates rows today; the commit table slice will write approved rates as tenant-scoped pricing corpus.

Availability

Brokers make the data usable

Moves and Source do not query random tables directly. A typed broker resolves the right tenant, pulls the approved corpus/context, applies precedence rules, and returns a compact evidence bundle to the agent.

Data type Parsed into Available to Precedence
Rate card Internal loaded-cost rows, vendor/SI bill rates, geo modifiers. Moves estimates, Source pricing normalization, BAFO questions. Client-approved rates over researched benchmark.
Modernization pack Archetypes, disposition rules, automation ranges, effort coefficients. Moves modernization baseline, Source SI scorecard, divergence report. Analyzer inventory over generic industry defaults.
Tenant context Evidence chunks, structured facts, provenance, audit trail. Intelligence, Moves, Source, Tower, Steward. Approved tenant evidence over global corpus.
Research ledger Source IDs, URLs, as-of dates, confidence, extraction status. All agents as provenance and fallback explanation. Official source rows over uncited assumptions.

How agents get smarter

The word training can be misleading. AbarVa does not need to fine-tune the base model every time a client uploads a file. The safer model is runtime grounding: each agent is given the right facts, patterns, policies, and examples at the moment it works.

Moves

Smarter estimates and choices

Moves uses rate cards, modernization archetypes, tenant inventory, value logic, and assumptions to produce planning ranges, not unsupported precision.

Source

Smarter vendor evaluation

Source uses the same corpus to normalize SI bids, compare sourcing models, flag divergence, and generate BAFO questions.

Steward

Smarter governance

Steward uses approvals, data quality, tenant isolation, and audit history to decide what the agent is allowed to rely on.

Agent input How it is controlled What the agent must show
Retrieved tenant evidence Tenant-scoped broker, approved-only filters, source locators. Client-specific citations and freshness.
Corpus pattern Versioned release record, source ledger, confidence tags. Pattern source and whether it is benchmark or client-specific.
Client override Approval queue, version history, rollback path. Override label and who approved it.
Missing evidence Validation findings and clarification workflow. Explicit gap, not a guessed answer.

How clients customize patterns

The near-term model is template-driven uploads. The future model is an admin studio where a client can review, edit, approve, version, and simulate overrides before they affect agents.

Now

Template uploads

Clients upload rate cards, context files, mappings, and evidence through governed templates. Bad rows are blocked before commit.

Next

Review and approve

Admins see parsed rows, validation gaps, provenance, confidence, and the exact agent surfaces that will be affected.

Future

Pattern Studio

Clients maintain their own approved patterns: rate cards, sourcing policies, modernization rules, risk weights, and scoring criteria.

Client action Example Control Agent impact
Upload a rate card Internal loaded-cost rates and vendor hourly bands. Parser validation, approval, versioning. Moves estimate uses client rates instead of benchmark.
Override a modernization rule Classify SAS workloads as re-architect, not replatform. Impact preview, approver signoff, rollback. Moves baseline and Source scorecard reflect client policy.
Update RFP weights Increase security from 10% to 20% for healthcare. Governed settings with audit trail. Source ranks SI bids with the client's priority model.
Retire a pattern Mark an old vendor benchmark as stale. Effective date, replacement rule, audit note. Agents stop using stale assumptions.

How hallucination is minimized

Hallucination is reduced by narrowing what the agent is allowed to rely on, making missing data visible, and forcing every important number or claim to carry provenance.

Evidence before assertion

Agent answers must cite tenant evidence, a corpus source, or a benchmark source. If none exists, the answer should say so.

Tenant isolation

Every retrieval and write path is scoped to the active client. Cross-tenant data cannot be used to fill a gap.

Confidence and freshness

Sources carry as-of dates, confidence, and extraction status. Stale or low-confidence evidence is labelled.

Validation before commit

Rates, enums, required fields, ranges, and provenance are checked before data becomes agent-available.

No silent fallback

If a client rate card is missing, the estimate can use a benchmark only if it is clearly labelled as benchmark.

Audit and replay

Data loads, approvals, agent source bundles, and release records make important answers reconstructable.

The board-level answer

AbarVa becomes smarter by expanding controlled knowledge, not by letting the model improvise. Research updates become versioned corpus. Client uploads become validated tenant context. Approved overrides change Moves and Source through brokered retrieval. Every important number must show where it came from, how current it is, whether it is client-specific, and what is still missing.
